name: Godello

lines.s10: Godello is the textured white of inland Galicia: ripe pear, white peach and wet stone on a round, medium to full body.
lines.s20: Godello comes from Valdeorras, a valley of slate hills in inland Galicia, and it almost died out in the 1970s. It gives a dry and rounded white that tastes of pear, white peach and lemon, with a stony finish.
lines.s45: Godello rewards the Chardonnay drinker who wants something new. It comes from Valdeorras, a valley of slate hills inland in Galicia, in north west Spain. It tastes of ripe pear, white peach and lemon, with a stony, faintly salty finish. It is dry and medium to full in body, with fresh acidity. Some is made crisp in steel, and the richer bottles rest on their spent yeast or in barrel for a creamy feel. It sits well beside roast fish, scallops or chicken. It had almost died out by the 1970s, until a local project replanted the valley from the few vines left.
lines.sale: Godello came back from a few surviving vines, and today it pours round and stony, with ripe pear and white peach. I would offer it to anyone who usually asks for Chardonnay, with the roast fish or the chicken.

glass.lead: Ripe pear, white peach and lemon over wet slate, round and medium to full, with a creamy feel where it has rested on its yeast.

ladder.where: The high slate slopes of Valdeorras and Ribeira Sacra
Monterrei, warmer and drier, near the Portuguese border

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus, alcohol medium to medium plus, body medium to full, with a round, textured feel and little or no new oak.

home.home: Valdeorras, a valley of slate slopes on the river Sil in eastern Galicia, with Bierzo, Ribeira Sacra and Monterrei beside it. Nearly lost by the 1970s, it was replanted from the few vines left. It is made fresh in steel, or kept on its lees or in barrel for a broader, creamier wine.
home.abroad: In Portugal it is Gouveio, a backbone of the Douro's dry whites and a grape of White Port; it was long called Verdelho there, though it is a different grape from Madeira's Verdelho. It is seldom planted beyond Iberia.

service.temp: 50 to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; a young, steel made bottle a little cooler.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a wider Burgundy bowl for a barrel aged bottle.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; open it and pour.
service.age: Fresh styles within three years; lees and barrel aged wines from old vines three to eight.

labels.means: The grape's home: a Galician denomination of slate slopes along the river Sil.
The neighbouring denomination in Castilla y León, upstream on the Sil, which shares the grape.
The same grape in Portugal, in the Douro's dry whites and in White Port.
On the lees: kept on its spent yeast for texture and a creamy note.
Fermented in barrel: a broader, richer style of the wine.

guest.q: I like white Burgundy. What would you pour me from Spain?
guest.a: Godello. It has a similar weight and roundness, with pear, white peach and a stony finish, and the richer bottles are aged on their lees or in barrel in much the same way.

guest.q: How is it different from Albariño?
guest.a: Albariño is lighter, more scented and saltier, from the coast. Godello comes from the inland valleys and is broader and quieter on the nose, a wine you notice more in the mouth.
Sometimes, and usually lightly. Most Godello is made in steel; the fuller bottles spend time on their lees or in barrel, which tends to add cream and texture more than vanilla.

compare.tell: Chardonnay, as white Burgundy, tends to show a plainer stamp of barrel and lees; Godello is quieter there, with pear, fennel and wet slate on a similar round body.
Albariño is more aromatic and saltier, lighter and higher in acidity; Godello is broader and stonier, felt more on the palate than the nose.
Verdejo is greener, with lime, cut grass, bay leaf and a bitter fennel finish; Godello is rounder and stonier, with pear and white peach.

cards.front: Godello: where is home, and what is the soil there?
cards.back: Valdeorras, on the river Sil in eastern Galicia, where slate slopes give the wine its stony edge. It also grows in Bierzo, Ribeira Sacra and Monterrei.

cards.front: What is Godello called in Portugal, and what does it make there?
cards.back: Gouveio. It is a backbone of the Douro's dry whites and one of the grapes of White Port.

cards.front: Godello almost died out: when, and how was it saved?
cards.back: By the 1970s little Godello was left in Valdeorras. A local project begun in 1974 studied the grape and replanted the valley from cuttings of the vines that remained.

questions.q: A blind white is straw gold, dry and medium to full, with ripe pear, white peach, fennel and wet slate, medium plus acidity and a faint creaminess but no vanilla. Which grape and origin fit it?
questions.exp: A broad, stony, quietly scented white with pear and a creamy feel from its lees points to Godello. Albariño would be lighter, more perfumed and saltier, with higher acidity.

questions.q: A guest who drinks unoaked white Burgundy asks for something Spanish with the same weight and a stony finish. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Godello gives a round, medium to full white of pear and wet slate, the nearest Spanish match for white Burgundy. Albariño is lighter and more perfumed, and Verdejo is greener.

questions.q: On a Portuguese list a guest finds a dry Douro white made from Gouveio and asks what that grape is called in Spain. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Gouveio is the Portuguese name of Godello, a backbone of the Douro's dry whites. Albariño is the grape Portugal calls Alvarinho, and its home there is Vinho Verde.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Valdeorras with Bierzo, Ribeira Sacra and Monterrei, and Gouveio in the Douro given as abroad.

No Codex record is contradicted. The profile, the dials and the region records for inland Galicia, Bierzo and the Douro supplied the fruit (white peach, green apple, quince, pear, fennel), the slate, the lees and barrel, the near loss by the 1970s and the name Gouveio.

The project of 1974 that replanted the grape stands on the Valdeorras council's own page and on Foods and Wines from Spain. The council's page is served at an http address, which the rule on sources refuses, so it is not listed. The first wine of Godello alone, in 1979, was left out: the council's page for it names a grower in its address.
Gouveio long called Verdelho in the Douro stands on Wines of Portugal; aniseed among the notes stands on the same page, fennel on the Codex's own note for Valdeorras.
Nectarine beside white peach, and bread dough beside fresh cream, are a taster's reading of the stone fruit and the lees the Codex names; no source read lists them by name.
The ladder has two rungs: Valdeorras and Ribeira Sacra as the cool ground, as the dials read the grape, and Monterrei as the warmer, drier valley the Codex's region record describes.
Structure: the dials read alcohol one step above Albariño, written here as medium to medium plus; the council gives about twelve and a half per cent as the average.
The redfish is the one dish from the Creole table.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after four fixes. The near loss of the 1970s and the project of 1974, Gouveio as the same vine in the Douro and in White Port, and the name Verdelho once worn by it there were confirmed.
changed: worlds.home.abroad: unrelated to Madeira's Verdelho now reads a different grape from Madeira's Verdelho. The DNA summaries read make both vines offspring of Savagnin, which would make them kin; a different grape is true on either reading.

lines.sale: Bring it to the guest who asks for Chardonnay now reads It is the bottle for anyone who usually asks for Chardonnay. The sale is said at the table, and the old sentence was an order to a server.
compare, the Chardonnay tell: it now opens Chardonnay, as white Burgundy, so that the tell names both grapes.

cards[2].back: only a few vines survived now reads little Godello was left, and the valley was replanted from cuttings of the vines that remained. The sources give a few hundred vines or a few dozen hectares and do not agree, so the card gives no count.
open: The forty five second line and the home line still say the few vines left: loose, and true of every count read.
Nectarine beside white peach and bread dough beside fresh cream are the author's reading and are not separately confirmed.
Whether Godello and Madeira's Verdelho are kin rests on secondary sources: see unsettled.
